title: "Causal Inference I: Counterfactuals, Randomisation, Matching"

## The question the first nine chapters could not answer

Every method so far has described an association and then, carefully, declined
to call it an effect. Chapter 2 insisted on "associated with" rather than
"causes". Chapter 6 showed the same association taking four different values
depending on which variation identified it. Chapter 9 produced two models with
identical fit and opposite causal arrows.

The reason for all that caution is that the question — *did the policy do
anything?* — is not a question about the data you have. It is a question about
data you do not have and cannot get.

This chapter answers it through three examples, each adding one idea. A
thousand simulated firms, where both answers are written down and a coin flip
can be watched beating self-selection. A real job-training programme, run as a
lottery, whose experimental answer lets matching on survey data be checked. And
a simulated training scheme in which matching first works and then, with one
unmeasured trait added, fails without any warning.

::: {.plate}
![](images/session-10-hume.jpg){fig-alt="David Hume** · **1711–1776."}

**David Hume** · **1711–1776**

Asked what entitles us to say one thing causes another, and did not find a satisfying answer. Neither has anyone since.

[Allan Ramsay, 1766. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.]{.plate-credit}
:::


::: {.archive}
[From the archive · Hume, 1739]{.archive-label}

David Hume asked what we actually observe when we say one thing causes another,
and answered: contiguity, succession, and constant conjunction. The billiard
ball moves; another moves after it; this has always happened. What we never
observe is the *necessary connection* — the thing that would make the second
event have to follow.

His second formulation is the one that founded modern causal inference, though
it took two centuries to be taken up. A cause, he wrote, is an object followed
by another, *and where, if the first object had not been, the second never had
existed*. That subordinate clause is a counterfactual: a statement about a world
that did not happen. It cannot be observed, in principle, for the same reason a
road not taken has no destination.

Hume treated this as a sceptical problem about knowledge. Modern statistics
treats it as a *missing data* problem, which turns out to be the more productive
framing — because missing data can sometimes be recovered, under assumptions you
can state, defend and occasionally test.
:::

## Potential outcomes

The framework that formalises Hume's clause is due to Neyman and, in its modern
form, to Rubin [@rubin1974]. For each unit $i$ define two quantities:

$$
Y_i(1) = \text{the outcome if unit } i \text{ is treated},
\qquad
Y_i(0) = \text{the outcome if it is not}.
$$

Both are properties of the unit, defined whether or not the treatment happens.
The causal effect *for that unit* is the difference

$$
\tau_i \thickspace=\thickspace Y_i(1) - Y_i(0),
$$

and it is exactly what Hume said we cannot observe: whichever treatment the unit
receives, the other potential outcome is missing, permanently and by
construction. This is the **fundamental problem of causal inference**
[@holland1986], and it means that no individual causal effect is ever
identified. What we can hope for is an *average*.

![The table you never get to see. Each firm has two potential outcomes; whichever choice it made, the other is missing, and so is its effect. The numbers come from the simulation later in this chapter, where, unusually, both columns exist.](images/decks/session-10-01-lecture-economist-assets-po-table.png){fig-alt="Six firms, each with sales growth with and without the programme. For each firm only one of the two is observed."}

::: {.definition}
[**ATE**]{.term} — average treatment effect, $\mathrm{E}[Y(1) - Y(0)]$
over the whole population. What would happen if everyone were treated versus no
one.
:::

::: {.definition}
[**ATT**]{.term} — average treatment effect on the treated,
$\mathrm{E}[Y(1) - Y(0) \mid T = 1]$. What the treatment did for those who
actually received it. Usually the policy-relevant quantity, and usually not
equal to the ATE.
:::

Now the arithmetic that explains why naive comparisons fail. What you can compute
from data is the difference in observed means. Add and subtract the same term:

$$
\underbrace{\mathrm{E}[Y \mid T{=}1] - \mathrm{E}[Y \mid T{=}0]}_{\text{what you can compute}}
=
\underbrace{\mathrm{E}[Y(1) - Y(0) \mid T{=}1]}_{\text{ATT}}
+
\underbrace{\mathrm{E}[Y(0) \mid T{=}1] - \mathrm{E}[Y(0) \mid T{=}0]}_{\text{selection bias}} .
$$

The second term is the difference between the treated and untreated groups *in
the absence of treatment*. If countries that adopt a policy would have differed
from those that did not even without it, the observed difference is the effect
plus that gap, and nothing in the data separates them.

![The decomposition in numbers, from the simulated firms below. The naive comparison says 5.33; the programme's effect is 2.00; the other 3.33 is how much faster the joining firms would have grown anyway.](images/decks/session-10-01-lecture-economist-assets-po-decomposition.png){fig-alt="A bar of 5.33 split into the effect, 2.00, and selection bias, 3.33."}

## Randomisation, and what it buys

Randomised assignment sets the selection term to zero, and it is worth being
precise about why. If treatment is assigned by a coin flip, then $T$ is
independent of everything about the unit — including $Y(0)$ and $Y(1)$ — so
$\mathrm{E}[Y(0) \mid T{=}1] = \mathrm{E}[Y(0) \mid T{=}0]$ and the
bias term vanishes.

Note what randomisation does *not* do. It does not make the groups identical; in
any finite sample they will differ, sometimes substantially. It makes them differ
*in a way unrelated to the outcome*, so the difference is noise rather than bias
— and noise is what standard errors are for. It also balances variables nobody
measured or thought of, which is the property no observational method can
replicate.

![Left: productivity drives both the decision to join and growth, so the comparison runs through a back door. Right: a coin decides, productivity can no longer reach the programme, and the back door is shut.](images/decks/session-10-01-lecture-economist-assets-dag-selection.png){fig-alt="Two causal diagrams: self-selection with a back door through productivity, and randomisation with a coin."}

When randomisation is unavailable, and in international business it usually is —
countries are not randomly assigned national strategies — the alternative is to
assume something strong enough to recover the same result.

::: {.definition}
[**Conditional independence**]{.term} (unconfoundedness, ignorability) — given a
set of covariates $X$, treatment is as good as random:
$\lbrace Y(0), Y(1)\rbrace \perp T \mid X$. Every determinant of both treatment and outcome
is in $X$. **This assumption is not testable**, because it concerns the missing
potential outcome.
:::

::: {.definition}
[**Overlap**]{.term} (common support) — for every value of $X$, the probability
of treatment is strictly between 0 and 1. If some countries would never adopt
under any circumstances, there is no comparison to be made for them, and an
estimate that includes them is extrapolating rather than comparing. Unlike
conditional independence, overlap **is** checkable.
:::

## Example 1 · Did the export programme work?

Everything above can be watched happening in a simulation, which is the one
setting where both potential outcomes exist. A thousand firms; a programme that
adds exactly two points to every firm's export growth; and a productivity that
nobody in the ministry observes, which raises growth with or without the
programme.

![Both potential outcomes for forty of the simulated firms. Each firm has two dots, two points apart: that gap is its effect. Both dots rise with productivity, because better firms grow faster whatever they do. Real data show one dot per firm.](images/decks/session-10-01-lecture-economist-assets-firms-two-outcomes.png){fig-alt="Forty firms, each with a grey dot for growth without the programme and a blue dot two points above for growth with it; both rise with productivity."}

```{python}
#| label: check-sim
#| code-summary: "Run it: a coin flip against self-selection, with the truth known"

import warnings
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
from sklearn.neighbors import NearestNeighbors

rng = np.random.default_rng(10)
n = 1000
productivity = rng.normal(0, 1, n)
sales_without = 10 + 3 * productivity + rng.normal(0, 2, n)
sales_with = sales_without + 2                         # the true effect, for every firm
applies = (productivity + rng.normal(0, 1, n) > 0.5).astype(int)

observed = np.where(applies == 1, sales_with, sales_without)
naive = observed[applies == 1].mean() - observed[applies == 0].mean()
bias = sales_without[applies == 1].mean() - sales_without[applies == 0].mean()
print(f"self-selection   naive {naive:.2f} = effect 2.00 + selection bias {bias:.2f}")

draws = []
for _ in range(1000):                                  # a thousand randomised experiments
    coin = rng.integers(0, 2, n)
    seen = np.where(coin == 1, sales_with, sales_without)
    draws.append(seen[coin == 1].mean() - seen[coin == 0].mean())
print(f"coin flip        mean of 1,000 estimates {np.mean(draws):.2f}, spread {np.std(draws):.2f}")
```

The two lines are the chapter's argument in miniature. Self-selection
overstates the effect by a factor of more than two and a half, and the excess is
exactly the selection term: the joining firms would have grown 3.33 points
faster without the programme. The coin is right on average and wrong in any
single draw by about a quarter of a point, which is noise, which a standard
error describes. The selection term cannot be computed in real data, since it
needs the column nobody sees; what *can* be computed is how different the groups
were before treatment, here about one standard deviation of productivity. That
comparison — balance — is the diagnostic the rest of the chapter is built on.

![Who chooses to join. The probability of joining rises with productivity, so the joiners (red, top) sit to the right of the non-joiners (grey, bottom): self-selection, in data.](images/decks/session-10-01-lecture-economist-assets-firms-who-joins.png){fig-alt="An S-shaped curve: the probability of joining rises with productivity."}

![Balance under a coin and under choice. With a coin the two groups have the same productivity before the programme; with choice the joiners were about one standard deviation more productive. The left panel is why randomisation works; the right is why the naive comparison fails.](images/decks/session-10-01-lecture-economist-assets-coin-vs-choice.png){fig-alt="Two histograms of productivity: overlapping under a coin, shifted under choice."}

**Example 1 in three sentences.** With a coin, the difference in means finds the
truth on average. When firms choose, the same difference says 5.33, of which 2 is
programme and 3.33 is selection. The selection bias itself is invisible; the
imbalance that causes it is not.

## Example 2 · LaLonde's test

The simulation knows the answer because it wrote it. A real data set that knows
the answer is rarer, and the most famous one is a job-training experiment.

The National Supported Work demonstration, run in the United States in
1976–77, assigned disadvantaged workers to a training placement **by lottery**.
The lottery's estimate of the effect on 1978 earnings is therefore credible.
LaLonde (1986) then did something that has shaped the field since: he kept the
trainees, threw away the lottery's controls, replaced them with people from
national surveys, and asked whether the estimators economists applied to survey
data would recover the experiment's answer. They did not, and the paper became
the standard argument for experiments. @dehejia1999 returned to the same data
with propensity-score matching and recovered it, and @smith2005 showed how
fragile that recovery is. The data are on Rajeev Dehejia's page at the NBER (National Bureau of Economic Research), and
`pd.read_stata` reads them directly.

![The design. The experiment gives the true effect; the survey version is the situation applied work is usually in.](images/decks/session-10-01-lecture-economist-assets-nsw-design.png){fig-alt="Left: the experiment, 185 trained and 260 untrained by lottery. Right: the same 185 trained compared with 15,992 people from a survey."}

```{python}
#| label: check-nsw-naive
#| code-summary: "Run it: the experiment's answer, and the naive survey comparison"

url = "https://users.nber.org/~rdehejia/data/"
nsw = pd.read_stata(url + "nsw_dw.dta")
cps = pd.read_stata(url + "cps_controls.dta")
X = ["age", "education", "black", "hispanic", "married", "nodegree", "re74", "re75"]

experiment = smf.ols("re78 ~ treat", data=nsw).fit()
print(f"experiment:  {experiment.params['treat']:+,.0f}  (SE {experiment.bse['treat']:,.0f})")

data = pd.concat([nsw[nsw["treat"] == 1], cps], ignore_index=True)
treated, control = data[data["treat"] == 1], data[data["treat"] == 0]
print(f"naive:       {treated['re78'].mean() - control['re78'].mean():+,.0f}")

regression = smf.ols("re78 ~ treat + " + " + ".join(X), data=data).fit()
print(f"regression:  {regression.params['treat']:+,.0f}   (same eight controls, linear)")

sd = np.sqrt((treated[X].var() + control[X].var()) / 2)
print("\nstandardised differences before matching:")
print(((treated[X].mean() - control[X].mean()) / sd).astype(float).round(2).to_string())
```

Training raised 1978 earnings by about \$1,800 in the experiment. Against the
survey, the naive comparison says it *cut* them by \$8,500: the wrong sign and
five times too large, because the survey's average worker earned \$14,000 a year
before the programme and the trainees under \$2,100. The standardised
differences put that in common units — the gap in means divided by the pooled
standard deviation — and most are between 0.7 and 2.4, against a convention
that calls anything under 0.1 balanced.

![Trainees and survey people on four characteristics. The survey's average worker is older, mostly married, has a diploma and earned nine times as much before the programme.](images/decks/session-10-01-lecture-economist-assets-nsw-profiles.png){fig-alt="Bars: age 26 against 33, 19% against 71% married, 71% against 30% without a diploma, 1975 earnings $1,532 against $13,651."}

Regression with all eight characteristics does much better, and is still off by
more than half. The reason is worth understanding, because it is what matching
fixes. A linear regression uses *every* survey respondent, including the
thousands earning \$20,000 and more who resemble no trainee, and lets a straight
line carry the comparison from them to the trainees. The estimate depends on that
line being right far outside the region where the trainees live.

![Earnings in 1978 against 1975. The survey people spread up to the survey's \$25,000 recording cap; the trainees bunch near zero. A regression learns its line from the grey cloud; matching uses only the blue survey people, who look like the trainees.](images/decks/session-10-01-lecture-economist-assets-nsw-regression.png){fig-alt="Scatter of survey people, trainees and matched controls, with a regression line through all survey people."}

## The propensity score, and a match that fails its check

@rosenbaum1983 proved that if treatment is as good as random given $X$, it is
as good as random given the single number $e(X) = P(T = 1 \mid X)$, the
**propensity score**. Eight dimensions collapse to one, and matching becomes the
nearest-neighbour problem of chapter 8 on one column.

![Matching on the score. Each treated unit is joined to the control with the closest score; controls unlike every treated unit are never used.](images/decks/session-10-01-lecture-economist-assets-matching-idea.png){fig-alt="Treated units above, controls below, on a propensity-score axis, each treated unit joined to its nearest control."}

```{python}
#| label: fig-nsw-overlap
#| code-summary: "Run it: estimate the score and check overlap"
#| fig-cap: "The propensity score in the two groups, on a logarithmic scale. Almost every survey respondent has a score near zero, but every bin that contains trainees also contains some survey respondents: the overlap needed for matching exists."

first = "treat ~ " + " + ".join(X)
data["pscore"] = smf.logit(first, data=data).fit(disp=0).predict(data)
treated, control = data[data["treat"] == 1], data[data["treat"] == 0]

bins = np.linspace(0, 0.5, 26)
plt.figure(figsize=(7, 3.4))
plt.hist(control["pscore"], bins=bins, alpha=0.6, label="survey (control)")
plt.hist(treated["pscore"], bins=bins, alpha=0.6, label="trained")
plt.yscale("log")
plt.xlabel("propensity score")
plt.legend()
plt.show()

print(f"score range, trained: {treated['pscore'].min():.3f} – {treated['pscore'].max():.3f}")
print(f"survey respondents with a score above 0.05: {(control['pscore'] > 0.05).sum()}")
```

Overlap is the checkable half of the identifying assumptions, and here it
holds, barely: of almost sixteen thousand survey respondents, a few hundred look
anything like a trainee. That is enough, because matching needs only one good
control per trainee.

```{python}
#| label: check-nsw-match1
#| code-summary: "Run it: match on the first score, then check balance"

nn = NearestNeighbors(n_neighbors=1).fit(control[["pscore"]])
distance, index = nn.kneighbors(treated[["pscore"]])
matched = control.iloc[index.ravel()]

print(f"{len(treated)} trainees, {matched.index.nunique()} distinct controls, "
      f"largest score gap {distance.max():.4f}")
print(((treated[X].mean() - matched[X].mean()) / sd).astype(float).round(2).to_string())
```

Matching with replacement lets a good control serve more than once, which is
why 185 trainees use fewer distinct controls. Balance has improved enormously
on earnings, race and schooling, but age is still out by 0.31: the logit has
treated the probability of training as moving in one direction with age, and it
does not. **This is the moment the procedure is designed for.** The response is
to change the score and check again, and to do it *without looking at the
outcome*, because a score chosen for the estimate it produces is a specification
search with a respectable name.

## A score that balances, and only then the outcome

```{python}
#| label: fig-nsw-balance
#| code-summary: "Run it: a better score, the balance check, and the ATT"
#| fig-cap: "Standardised differences before matching (blue) and after matching on the improved score (orange). The dashed lines mark ±0.1. Every covariate ends inside them."

better = first + " + I(age**2) + I(re74 == 0) + I(re75 == 0)"
data["pscore"] = smf.logit(better, data=data).fit(disp=0).predict(data)
treated, control = data[data["treat"] == 1], data[data["treat"] == 0]
nn = NearestNeighbors(n_neighbors=1).fit(control[["pscore"]])
distance, index = nn.kneighbors(treated[["pscore"]])
matched = control.iloc[index.ravel()]

before = (treated[X].mean() - control[X].mean()) / sd
after = (treated[X].mean() - matched[X].mean()) / sd
plt.figure(figsize=(7, 3.6))
plt.scatter(before, X, label="before")
plt.scatter(after, X, label="after")
plt.axvline(-0.1, color="grey", linestyle="--")
plt.axvline(0.1, color="grey", linestyle="--")
plt.xlabel("standardised difference")
plt.legend()
plt.show()

att = treated["re78"].mean() - matched["re78"].mean()
print(f"largest |difference| after matching: {after.abs().max():.2f}")
print(f"ATT by matching: {att:+,.0f}    experiment: {experiment.params['treat']:+,.0f}")
```

Age squared lets the probability of training rise and fall with age; the two
indicators mark people who earned nothing in 1974 or 1975, which is most
trainees and few survey respondents. With them, every standardised difference
sits inside 0.1. The figure — a **love plot** — is the evidence a reader needs,
and it is the evidence to report, rather than the logit's coefficients or fit,
which are a means and not an end.

Only now is the outcome looked at. The matched ATT is about \$2,000, within a
third of a standard error of the experiment.

![What a match looks like: five trainees, each above the survey person matched to them. Score, age, schooling and earnings before training are close; earnings after are compared. Single pairs are noisy; only the average over all 185 is the estimate.](images/decks/session-10-01-lecture-economist-assets-nsw-pairs.png){fig-alt="Five trainee and match pairs with their scores, ages, schooling and earnings in 1975 and 1978."}

![Every estimate on one axis. Both matching estimates fall inside the experiment's 95% interval; the naive comparison has the wrong sign, and the linear regression is pulled down by respondents who resemble no trainee.](images/decks/session-10-01-lecture-economist-assets-nsw-estimates.png){fig-alt="Five estimates on one axis: naive −8,498, regression +699, first matching +1,831, balanced matching +2,001, and the experiment +1,794 with its 95% interval."}

Two cautions keep this from being a triumph. The first is uncertainty. The
standard error printed by a regression on the matched sample ignores that the
score was estimated and that controls were reused; a bootstrap that redoes the
whole procedure is the honest version.

```{python}
#| label: check-nsw-bootstrap
#| code-summary: "Run it: bootstrap the whole matching procedure"

estimates = []
for b in range(200):
    t = treated.sample(len(treated), replace=True, random_state=b)
    c = control.sample(len(control), replace=True, random_state=1000 + b)
    nn_b = NearestNeighbors(n_neighbors=1).fit(c[["pscore"]])
    _, idx = nn_b.kneighbors(t[["pscore"]])
    estimates.append(t["re78"].mean() - c.iloc[idx.ravel()]["re78"].mean())
print(f"bootstrap standard error of the ATT: {np.std(estimates):,.0f}")
print(f"95% interval: {np.percentile(estimates, 2.5):+,.0f} to {np.percentile(estimates, 97.5):+,.0f}")
```

(Strictly the score should be re-estimated inside each replication too; holding
it fixed, as here, keeps the cell short and understates the spread a little.)
The interval is wide — the matched estimate rests on 185 trainees and a much
smaller number of distinct controls — and it comfortably contains the
experimental answer. It also, worth saying plainly, reaches zero: on the survey
data alone, matching cannot rule out that training did nothing, which the
experiment, with its own controls, could.

The second caution is that one success is not a guarantee. LaLonde's paper used
a second survey, the Panel Study of Income Dynamics, and the same procedure
there tells a less tidy story.

```{python}
#| label: check-nsw-psid
#| code-summary: "Run it: the same recipe with the other survey"

psid = pd.read_stata(url + "psid_controls.dta")
data2 = pd.concat([nsw[nsw["treat"] == 1], psid], ignore_index=True)
data2["pscore"] = smf.logit(better, data=data2).fit(disp=0).predict(data2)
t2, c2 = data2[data2["treat"] == 1], data2[data2["treat"] == 0]
nn2 = NearestNeighbors(n_neighbors=1).fit(c2[["pscore"]])
_, idx2 = nn2.kneighbors(t2[["pscore"]])
m2 = c2.iloc[idx2.ravel()]
sd2 = np.sqrt((t2[X].var() + c2[X].var()) / 2)

print(f"naive {t2['re78'].mean() - c2['re78'].mean():+,.0f}   "
      f"ATT {t2['re78'].mean() - m2['re78'].mean():+,.0f}   "
      f"distinct controls {m2.index.nunique()}")
print(((t2[X].mean() - m2[X].mean()) / sd2).astype(float).round(2).to_string())
```

The estimate is again close to the experiment, but balance is not achieved:
four covariates stay outside 0.1, schooling and the no-diploma indicator by the
most, and the whole match rests on a few dozen distinct controls. A careful analyst would report that, and
would not present the closeness of the number as vindication, because in real
work there is no experiment to compare with. @smith2005 make the general point:
the Dehejia–Wahba success depends on which subsample and which score, and the
lesson is about the conditions under which matching works — rich pre-treatment
earnings, comparison groups from the same labour market — rather than about
matching as such.

**Example 2 in three sentences.** The experiment says training raised 1978
earnings by about \$1,800; against survey controls, the naive comparison says
−\$8,500. A propensity score, an overlap check and a balance check, all settled
before the outcome is seen, bring matching to about \$2,000, while a linear
regression on the same variables misses by more than half. It worked because two
years of pre-programme earnings capture most of what decided who enrolled.

## The control that changes the question

Deciding what goes into the score is a claim about causal structure. The rule
is to condition only on variables fixed **before** treatment, and the reason is
clearest when it is broken.

![A confounder, measured before treatment, opens a back door and should be controlled for. A mediator, created by the treatment, carries part of the effect, and controlling for it removes that part.](images/decks/session-10-01-lecture-economist-assets-dag-bad-control.png){fig-alt="Left: firm size before the programme causes both joining and growth. Right: new export contracts are caused by the programme and cause growth."}

```{python}
#| label: check-mediator
#| code-summary: "Run it: controlling for a mediator"

rng = np.random.default_rng(10)
size = rng.normal(0, 1, n)                                  # before the programme
joins = (size + rng.normal(0, 1, n) > 0.5).astype(int)
contracts = 1.5 * joins + rng.normal(0, 1, n)               # created by the programme
growth = 10 + 2 * size + 0.5 * joins + 1.0 * contracts + rng.normal(0, 2, n)
firms = pd.DataFrame({"size": size, "joins": joins, "contracts": contracts, "growth": growth})

for formula in ["growth ~ joins", "growth ~ joins + size", "growth ~ joins + size + contracts"]:
    print(f"{formula:36} {smf.ols(formula, data=firms).fit().params['joins']:.2f}")
print("true total effect: 0.5 direct + 1.5 × 1.0 through contracts = 2.0")
```

Without controls, selection on size inflates the estimate. Controlling for size
— a confounder, fixed before the programme — recovers the total effect of 2.
Adding new export contracts, which the programme itself creates, drops the
estimate to the direct effect alone, because conditioning on a mediator holds
fixed the channel through which most of the effect travels. The regression is
not wrong; it answers a different and usually uninteresting question. The
related case of a **collider**, a common consequence of treatment and outcome,
is worse: conditioning on it *creates* an association that does not exist
[@elwert2014]. @cinelli2022 is the short guide worth keeping beside the
keyboard.

::: {.warn}
**"Closer to the right answer" is not the same as "the right method."** In real
work the truth is unknown, so the only evidence available is whether the
procedure is justified. A procedure that is wrong for a reason you can state will
be wrong by an unknown amount in the next dataset, and no diagnostic will
announce it.
:::

## Example 3 · Does analytics training raise performance?

Matching came within \$210 of the experiment on the CPS, the Current Population Survey. The third example shows
why that is not the same as solving the problem, in a setting from the
human-resources side of international business. A large organisation offers its
employees an advanced data-analytics course; taking it is voluntary; the human-resources (HR)
analytics team wants to know whether it raises a standardised annual performance
score. The HR file records age, education and experience. It does not record
motivation.

The data are simulated, 800 employees, so the truth is known: the course adds 5
points to everyone. Older and more educated employees are more likely to enrol.
In version A that is all that drives enrolment. In version B motivated employees
also enrol more, and motivation raises performance on its own. The same matching
procedure — a logit score on the three recorded variables, one nearest neighbour,
a balance check — is applied to both.

![Who enrols. In A, everything that decides enrolment is in the HR file; in B, motivation, which the file does not record, also decides it and raises performance on its own.](images/decks/session-10-01-lecture-economist-assets-hr-dag.png){fig-alt="Two causal diagrams for versions A and B of the HR example."}

```{python}
#| label: check-hr
#| code-summary: "Run it: the same matching, with and without an unmeasured confounder"

rng = np.random.default_rng(10)
n_staff = 800
age = rng.normal(40, 10, n_staff).round()
education = rng.normal(14, 2, n_staff).round()
experience = np.clip(age - 6 - education + rng.normal(0, 3, n_staff), 0, None).round()
motivation = rng.normal(0, 1, n_staff)                          # never in the HR file
perf_without = (50 + 0.3 * experience + 1.5 * (education - 14) + 4 * motivation
                + rng.normal(0, 5, n_staff))
perf_with = perf_without + 5                                    # the truth: +5

records = -1 + 0.05 * (age - 40) + 0.4 * (education - 14) + 0.03 * (experience - 20)
cols = ["age", "education", "experience"]
for version, index_ in [("A", records), ("B", records + 1.2 * motivation)]:
    draw = np.random.default_rng(11)
    enrol = (draw.uniform(size=n_staff) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-index_))).astype(int)
    staff = pd.DataFrame({"age": age, "education": education, "experience": experience,
                          "treat": enrol, "motivation": motivation,
                          "performance": np.where(enrol == 1, perf_with, perf_without)})
    staff["pscore"] = smf.logit("treat ~ age + education + experience",
                                data=staff).fit(disp=0).predict(staff)
    t, c = staff[staff["treat"] == 1], staff[staff["treat"] == 0]
    _, idx = NearestNeighbors(n_neighbors=1).fit(c[["pscore"]]).kneighbors(t[["pscore"]])
    m = c.iloc[idx.ravel()]
    sd_s = np.sqrt((t[cols + ["motivation"]].var() + c[cols + ["motivation"]].var()) / 2)
    gaps = (t[cols + ["motivation"]].mean() - m[cols + ["motivation"]].mean()) / sd_s
    print(f"version {version}: naive {t['performance'].mean() - c['performance'].mean():5.2f}"
          f"   matched {t['performance'].mean() - m['performance'].mean():5.2f}   (truth 5)")
    print("   standardised differences after matching:", gaps.round(2).to_dict())
```

![The same procedure on the two versions. In A, matching moves the estimate from 8.6 to 5.3, close to the truth; in B it stops at 9.0.](images/decks/session-10-01-lecture-economist-assets-hr-estimates.png){fig-alt="Version A: naive 8.6, matched 5.3; version B: naive 11.5, matched 9.0; truth 5."}

In version A, matching does what it did on LaLonde's data: the naive comparison
says 8.6 and the matched estimate 5.3. In version B, the same steps produce the
same reassuring balance table and an estimate of 9.0, nearly double the truth.
The reason is in the last column of the balance check, the one the analyst cannot
compute.

![Balance after matching in version B. The three recorded variables are inside ±0.1; motivation, which is not in the file, is off by more than a standard deviation.](images/decks/session-10-01-lecture-economist-assets-hr-hidden.png){fig-alt="Age, education and experience within 0.1 after matching; motivation off by 1.14."}

Balance can only be checked on what was measured, and conditional independence
is a claim about everything else. On LaLonde's data, matching worked because the
survey records two years of earnings before the programme, which capture most of
what decided who enrolled. Here nothing in the file captures motivation, and no
score built from the file can recover the experiment that was never run.

**Example 3 in three sentences.** When enrolment depends on what the HR file
records, matching recovers the course's effect. When motivation also drives it,
matching still balances everything in the file and still reports a number, nearly
double the truth. The difference between the two versions is invisible in the
data; it is an argument about who enrols and why.

## Matching or regression?

Matching and regression adjustment are the *same assumption* in different
clothing: both require that conditioning on the observed covariates suffices.
They differ in how they use it.

| | Regression on the confounders | Matching on the propensity score |
|---|---|---|
| **Comparison** | every treated unit against a line fitted through all controls | each treated unit against the controls most like it |
| **Overlap** | not checked; extrapolates where no comparable control exists | visible in the score's distribution |
| **Functional form** | must be right — linear unless specified otherwise | needs only a score that balances |
| **Order of work** | the outcome sits in the same model as the controls | the design is fixed, by balance, before the outcome is seen |
| **In this chapter** | LaLonde: +\$699 | LaLonde: +\$2,001 (experiment +\$1,794) |

When overlap is good and the relations are close to linear, the two agree: in
version A of Example 3 a regression on the three recorded variables gives about
4.6. When overlap is poor, as with LaLonde's survey, regression's line carries
the comparison into regions with no trainees and matching is the safer device.
When the assumption itself fails, as in version B, neither helps, and both fail
in the same direction.

## What none of this fixes

Example 3 cannot be diagnosed from the data, so the honest response is to ask how
wrong the assumption could be. Sensitivity
analysis asks how strong an unobserved confounder would have to be — how
strongly associated with both treatment and outcome — to overturn the
conclusion. If the answer is "about as strong as the covariates already
controlled for", the finding is fragile. If it is "stronger than any known
determinant", it is robust. Either way the reader learns something a point
estimate does not tell them.

One caution about the method itself. Propensity-score matching is the most
popular approach here and not the best one: matching on a scalar score discards
information and can *increase* imbalance as the caliper tightens, a pathology
documented at length by @king2019. Matching directly on the covariates, or
weighting rather than matching, generally does better. The score remains a good
diagnostic for overlap even where it is a poor matching device.

Chapter 11 takes the other route: rather than assuming the confounders are all
observed, it uses the structure of *when* treatment arrived to difference the
unobserved ones away.

## A short review of the literature

::: {.lit}
The potential-outcomes notation is @rubin1974, though the idea traces to Neyman's
1923 work on agricultural experiments. @holland1986 named the fundamental problem
and drew the boundary the discipline still uses — "no causation without
manipulation" — which remains contested and clarifying.

LaLonde's 1986 comparison of experimental and non-experimental estimates of a
job-training programme is the benchmark the matching literature is still judged
against; @dehejia1999 showed propensity-score matching recovering the
experimental answer, and @smith2005 showed how much that depends on the sample
and the specification.

@rosenbaum1983 proved the result that made observational adjustment tractable:
if treatment is unconfounded given a covariate vector, it is unconfounded given
the scalar propensity score alone, so a many-dimensional matching problem
collapses to one dimension. @imbens2004 surveys the estimators that followed and
@stuart2010 is the practical review, covering matching, weighting and the
diagnostics that should accompany them.

The corrective literature is as important as the constructive one. @king2019
argues that propensity-score matching specifically — as opposed to matching in
general — often increases imbalance and should be replaced by methods that match
on covariates directly. @elwert2014 sets out endogenous selection bias, the
family of errors created by conditioning on colliders, and @cinelli2022 gives the
compact treatment of which controls help and which do damage.
:::

## What to report

1. **The estimand, named.** ATE or ATT — they answer different questions and
   matching usually estimates the second.
2. **The identifying assumption, in words.** Which variables are claimed to
   close every path from treatment to outcome, and why that list is complete.
   This is an argument, not a table.
3. **Balance before and after**, for every covariate, with standardised
   differences — a love plot. Not the propensity model's coefficients or its
   fit. And say that the score was settled before the outcome was looked at.
4. **Overlap**, with the range of the score in both groups, and what you did
   about units outside common support.
5. **The naive estimate alongside the adjusted one.** The distance between them
   is the size of the selection problem, and hiding it hides the reason for the
   analysis.
6. **A sensitivity analysis.** How strong an unobserved confounder would need to
   be to overturn the result.
7. **That every control is pre-treatment**, and that you know it. If a covariate
   is measured after treatment, say why it is not a mediator or a collider — and
   if you cannot, drop it, even when it improves the number.
